name: Shawl lapel

lead: The shawl lapel is a single unbroken curve running from the collar down the front of a jacket, with no step or peak. It is most associated with dinner jackets and tuxedos, where its soft line gives a polished evening look.
For appearance, lapel shape changes the lines of the upper body. A smooth curve reads as soft and elegant, in contrast to the angled points of a peak lapel or the step of a notch lapel.

paras: People choose it when buying or renting a tuxedo or dinner jacket, or when having evening wear made. It is commonly worn with a bow tie and formal shirt, and is also seen on mess jackets and some modern fashion pieces.
No health risks. As with any formalwear, fit across the shoulders and chest determines how the lapel lies.

chain: Soft, sleek line down the chest
angle.text: The smooth curve gives a tuxedo or dinner jacket a softer, more fluid front than angled lapels. Wearers choose it for formal evenings and black-tie events.

lead: A shawl lapel, also called a shawl collar or roll collar, is a lapel formed as a single unbroken curve with no notch and no point.[1] It originated on the Victorian smoking jacket, an informal evening garment, and is now most common on dinner jackets and tuxedos and also appears on mess jackets.[1]

Style guides treat lapel shape as a way to shape the look of a jacket. The shawl is the only one of the three common types, alongside notched and peaked, that is not defined by an angle: notched lapels are standard on business suits and blazers, while peaked lapels are the most formal and nearly always used on double-breasted jackets.[1] People who choose a shawl lapel are typically after a smooth, rounded evening silhouette.

paras: Where a notched lapel has a step where lapel meets collar and a peaked lapel has points angled upward, the shawl lapel is one continuous curve.[1] It is often made in a contrasting fabric such as satin on tuxedos.
The style began on the Victorian smoking jacket, an informal evening garment, and was later made in both more and less formal versions.[1]
No studies found. The term 'shawl lapel' also appears in cardiac surgery as the name of an aortic remodeling technique, which is unrelated to clothing.
